title: Joining Jimmy Archey's Dixieland band at Jimmy Ryan's
summary: Schaap leaps ahead to Europe. Waters tells how a Brooklyn gig with Henry Goodwin led to a job at Jimmy Ryan's after he agreed to play clarinet and soprano in Archey's Dixieland band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: OK, Benny, this is the point where we're gonna leap forward so we don't have to squeeze this in at the end. I'd like to take you back 30 years, place you on 52nd Street, playing at Jimmy Ryan's with Jimmy Archey's band. And Archey informs the band and yourself that you're going to Europe, and this ushers in a 30 year stretch of time, in fact one of the longest expatriacies of an American jazz musician. And indeed you have now become the patriarch of the expatriates, 'cause you A: started late and stayed long and are still going strong at 80. So we're trying to get at the story of your 30 year European experience starting at the beginning. So why don't you take us right back to when, the gig - playing with Archey at Ryan's and -
Right, and then finding out you're going to Europe and everything.

OK, I can do that, I think [ ]. And the first thing, I played a gig with, in New York, I've lived in Philadelphia, that's the first thing, I lived with a girlfriend of mine. But I did very well [ ] when I was in Philadelphia. And I just came to New York at Jimmy Ryan's, just, without one of my own, see. No, wrong again. I came on a gig with Henry Goodwin in Brooklyn, his band, I forget who was -
The trumpet player who played with -

with [ ], he died not too long ago. See, so anyway I played this gig, I think it was Brooklyn. And I was playing saxophone but I had the clarinet always, 'cause I had 'em both in the same case. So I didn't play because he didn't seem to be called for, to play in particular. So anyway - then he asked me, could I play clarinet. So I told him "No, I'm not exactly a clarinetist". I said "I started on clarinet but I'm not exactly a clarinetist, but I can play a certain amount, you know". So he said "If you can play clarinet you have a job at Jimmy Ryan's, 'cause Bob Wilber is going to New Orleans for three years and Jimmy Archey was asked to take charge of the band, to go into Jimmy Ryan's". And that's I first started, see. So I said "No, I'm not exactly a clarinetist", but I said "but I may be able to hold a job". So finally I got this, they happened to call up on a Monday night, when they have sessions at Jimmy Ryan. So I come up on a Monday night and I jam. And I jam on the clarinet, it was not too bad, see. Good enough. But they were really gonna get Omer Simeon, but he couldn't join on account of that 6 month period of waiting on the Union. Otherwise, they were gonna use Omer as a clarinetist, as we all know. See, so - but I got, I did well enough to get the job. Then in the meantime Jimmy asked, could I play soprano. Well, I said "Yes" because I played soprano at [ ], you know. I said "Yes, I can play soprano". See, but I said "I don't have any, though". So he said "Can you get one?" I said "Yeah, I can get one". So he, so I got, I bought a soprano. And then when I got the soprano I couldn't find a mouthpiece. So I went down in the Bowery, out there in Chinatown part of New York and found one of those old mouthpieces they [ ], in a barrel, see. So I go up, I got the mouthpiece that sound real good, see. So then I joined the band. So we stayed, I stayed in the band about three years. And we had a Dixieland band. We were playing Dixieland numbers - "Fidgety Feet", "That's A Plenty", "Dixieland One-step", "Tiger Rag", "High Society". We were playing, it was a Dixieland band. And I never played Dixieland before, my first time, see, in my whole life, see. But so, it was real hard for me at first for the clarinet -

not the saxophone [ ], the soprano's just a saxophone player, I mean just a saxophone. But the clarinet was a little difficulty for me. So (cough) I never been lazy - so if I can't do something I'd practice, I work it out. So I worked out all the numbers, you know, see, that I didn't know so well. They got quite a main stay in the band, I mean, not only [ ] and stuff and chard is there (laughs) in the end, particularly when I got to soprano too, you know. So I got so I could play all these numbers, and quite a success. So I stayed there three years.
